title: For loops
summary: Count with for, walk through a string with foreach, nest loops, and dodge the off-by-one error.

steps.title: Counting in one line
body: Counting loops always have the same three chores: create a counter, test it, change it. With `while` those are scattered over three places, and forgetting the last one gives an infinite loop.
`for` puts all three in the header:
prints `0`, `1`, `2`. The header has three parts, separated by `;`:
2. `i < 3` is checked **before every pass**. When it is false the loop ends.
The step can be anything: `i--` counts down, `i += 2` skips every other number. The counter `i` only exists inside the loop.

steps.prompt: In `for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) { ... }`, when does each part run?
pairs: before every pass, to decide whether to go on
once per pass, while the condition holds

steps.explain: `i` starts at 2 and goes up by 3: 2, 5, 8. The next value, 11, fails `i <= 8`. `Write` puts them all on one line.

steps.prompt: Complete the loop so it counts down `10, 9, 8 ... 1`.
steps.explain: Start at 10, keep going while `i` is still 1 or more, and step down. With `>` the loop would stop at 2.

steps.title: The off-by-one error
body: The most common loop bug is running **one pass too many or one too few**. It has a name: the off-by-one error.
It comes from two small choices: where you start, and whether you write `<` or `<=`.
The first two are the standard shapes. Use `0` with `<` when you just need *n passes*. Use `1` with `<=` when you need the numbers *1 to n* themselves.
> **Tip:** when a loop misbehaves, check the first and the last value of the counter by hand.

steps.title: foreach: every item, no counter
body: A string is a sequence of `char` values. To visit each one you do not need a counter at all:
prints `c`, `a`, `t` on separate lines. Read it as *for each char `c` in `word`*. On every pass `c` holds the next character.

With no counter there is nothing to get off by one. Reach for `foreach` whenever you want **every item** and do not care about its position. It works on every collection you will meet in the next module.

steps.explain: The loop looks at b, a, n, a, n, a in turn and counts the three that equal `'a'`. A `char` is written with single quotes.

steps.title: Loops inside loops
body: A loop body can hold any statements, including another loop. For **every** pass of the outer loop, the inner loop runs **from start to finish**.
The inner body ran 2 x 3 = 6 times. Nested loops are the natural shape for anything with rows and columns: grids, tables, game boards.
`Console.WriteLine()` with nothing in the parentheses just ends the current line.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines to print **2 rows of 3 stars**. The indentation shows what belongs inside what.
steps.explain: The outer loop makes the rows. The inner loop writes one row of stars, and the `WriteLine()` after it ends that row before the next begins.

steps.title: Hollow box
prompt: Read a `width`, then a `height`, and draw a box of that size. The border is made of `#`, the inside is spaces.
You may assume both numbers are at least 1.
starter: // Outer loop: one pass per row
//   Inner loop: one pass per column, write "#" or " "
solution: if (row == 1 || row == height || col == 1 || col == width)
hints: Start by drawing a **solid** box: an outer loop over rows, an inner loop over columns writing `#`, and `Console.WriteLine()` after the inner loop.
A position is on the border when it is in the first or last row, or the first or last column.
`if (row == 1 || row == height || col == 1 || col == width)` write `#`, otherwise write a space.

steps.title: A bar for the week chart
prompt: **Sidekick piece: the bars of `sk week`.** Each day of your week is drawn as a bar, `#` for done and `.` for the
rest. Your code becomes the body of `static string Bar(int value, int max, int width)`. The three are given; put
a string of exactly `width` characters in `result`:
- `filled = value * width / max` (whole numbers), or `0` when `max` is `0`;
- no more than `width` and no less than `0`;
- `filled` times `#`, then `.` for the rest. Build it with a `for` loop that adds one character per pass.
starter: // value, max and width are given. result starts as "".
template: static string Bar(int value, int max, int width)
Dojo.Eq("over the max is capped", "####", Bar(15, 10, 4));

require.message: Builds the bar with a for loop

hints: Work out `filled` first with three `if`s: the division (only when `max > 0`), then the cap at `width`, then the floor at `0`.
`for (int i = 0; i < width; i++)` visits every position of the bar.
